title: Odd fluids from chiral cellular automata
authors: Andrew A. Allocca, Shiva Heidari, Thomas Iadecola, Armin Rahmani, Pouyan Ghaemi, Sriram Ganeshan
abstract: Cellular automata are discrete dynamical systems defined on a lattice, in which each site carries a finite set of states that evolve in time according to local deterministic rules. An important application of cellular automata is in lattice gas models of fluids, where the cellular automaton framework provides a particle-based microscopic description of hydrodynamic behavior. The macroscopic fluid equations emerge after coarse-graining over many lattice sites and time steps, offering a bottom-up route to hydrodynamics. A celebrated example is the Frisch-Hasslacher-Pomeau (FHP) model, an automaton defined on a two-dimensional triangular lattice that yields the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations upon coarse-graining. In this work, we construct a parity-breaking generalization of the FHP model through two modifications: introducing chiral two-body collision rules and systematically rotating particle velocities to mimic the effect of a background magnetic field. We show that this automaton yields a hydrodynamic model with odd viscosity, a transverse transport coefficient that is a hallmark of odd fluids. We verify the analytical transport coefficients using Poiseuille-flow simulations of the chiral FHP automaton. Our results demonstrate that the chiral automaton introduced here provides a bridge between microscopic parity-breaking scattering processes and macroscopic odd-fluid hydrodynamics.
summary: This work develops a chiral generalization of the FHP lattice gas automaton to model fluids exhibiting odd viscosity. By introducing asymmetric scattering rules, the authors show that microscopic parity violation leads directly to macroscopic Hall viscosity ($\eta_H$). The methodology successfully bridges discrete particle dynamics with continuum hydrodynamics via rigorous theoretical expansion and simulation.
main_problem: The study aims to understand how microscopic chiral properties, encoded in local particle interactions within a lattice gas automaton, manifest as macroscopic odd-fluid behavior.
main_result: The authors successfully constructed a parity-breaking cellular automaton that yields continuum hydrodynamic equations exhibiting non-zero Hall viscosity ($\eta_H$), linking discrete chirality rules to measurable transport coefficients.
method: The derivation involves constructing a chiral generalization of the FHP lattice gas model and employing a Chapman-Enskog expansion on the associated Boltzmann equation to extract macroscopic transport coefficients.
model_or_system: The system is a 2D triangular lattice modeled by a cellular automaton, which undergoes discrete time evolution via collision (including asymmetric two-body chiral scattering) and streaming steps, with an optional rotation mimicking a magnetic field.
key_observables: Odd viscosity ($\eta_H$), shear viscosity ($\eta$), and the full stress tensor components ($\sigma_{ij}$), measured through Poiseuille flow simulations.
important_parameters: Chirality parameter ($p$) governing collision asymmetry, external magnetic field strength ($B$), and the small expansion parameter ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on a Chapman-Enskog expansion in multiple scales ($\epsilon$) and assumes that the system can be coarse-grained into continuum hydrodynamics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the time evolution rules (streaming, 3-body, chiral 2-body collisions) and compare simulated vs. analytically predicted values for shear and Hall viscosities as a function of the chirality parameter $p$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the microscopic chiral automaton dynamics to deriving the continuum hydrodynamic equations via Chapman-Enskog expansion, culminating in analytical predictions and numerical verification of both standard and odd transport coefficients.
why_interesting: While focused on classical fluid dynamics, the methodology—deriving macroscopic symmetries (or lack thereof) from explicit micro-rules involving broken parity—is highly relevant to understanding symmetry breaking in quantum many-body systems or non-equilibrium quantum field theories.
